title: Taxonomy of Education Disruptors (2022 Edition)
author: Peter Greene
summary: Peter Greene sorts the post-reform landscape into a field guide of education disruptors: data miners, charter advocates, parents' rights activists, voucher fans, techno-education vendors, free marketeers, test-o-crats and a hopeful remnant who simply want schools to work. His argument is that the old label of reformer no longer fits, because much of the reform agenda, high-stakes testing above all, is now the status quo and the coalitions behind it have fractured. He reads each faction through its real motive rather than its rhetoric, arguing for example that parents' rights campaigners are less interested in choice than in dismantling the public system. He closes with a cautious hope that, as the most destructive disruptors drift to the fringe, defenders of public schools and former reformers could talk about helping students learn. The piece is characteristic Greene: school-policy commentary written from the teacher's side of the fence.
points: Greene argues the term reformer is obsolete because high-stakes testing and other reform ideas are now the status quo.
He warns that every digitized school tool feeds a data industry and that vague promises to share data only with trusted partners are meaningless.
He claims voucher and parents' rights advocacy share a goal of treating education as a private commodity, not a public good.
He holds that a free market is a poor fit for any essential service that must reach every member of society.
He ends with a hope that people who want education to help students become fully human may now find common ground.
quotes: Every time a digitized education tool shows up, someone should be asking what will happen to the data it collects. How will it be kept secure? How will it be shared?

Pity the charter school advocates. When vouchers were off the table, charters had the support of a lot of folks who hoped they would be a Next Best Thing, a foot in the door. But now that vouchers are having their day in state legislators, Freedom Fans have left charters behind.

Implicit in this crowds' beliefs is that only certain values should be represented in education. They are not pro-choice, just as they are not pro-democracy. Education (and government) are legitimate only when they align with the Right Values.
The free market is a lousy match for any critical human service. It's not evil; it's just a bad match for any system that needs to deliver an essential service to all members of society.

Nothing pushed on education since the days of A Nation At Risk has done more damage to actual education than high stakes testing. It should be fought at every possible level, from pointing out that the pursuit of test scores has not improved anything to demanding that people say "raise test scores" instead of "improve student achievement.

Much of what reformsters pushed is now status quo (e.g. high stakes testing), which means that I'm technically an advocate for education reform. Meanwhile, many folks whose predecessors were ed reformsters are no longer claiming that mantle.
